scenario: A 76-year-old woman presented with a palpable left axillary mass. When she was 36 years old, she underwent a hysterectomy due to abnormal uterine bleeding and was taking estradiol to control postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms for the past 20 years. Bilateral diagnostic mammography revealed a high-density irregular mass in the left axilla with no nodules, architectural distortions, or microcalcifications in the breasts. Ultrasonography of the left breast showed a 4.6-cm lobulated mixed cystic and solid left axillary mass. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging showed an enhancing 5.2-cm left axillary mass with no breast lesions (Figure 1A). The biopsy examination indicated high-grade adenocarcinoma with papillary features (estrogen receptor– and progesterone receptor–positive, ERBB2 [formerly HER2]–negative, and a high Ki67 index). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography revealed only high uptake in the left axilla region. The patient was treated at an outside hospital with neoadjuvant dose-dense doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, followed by weekly paclitaxel for 10 weeks. She then transferred her care to our center for surgical management. We requested the pathology slides for review at our laboratory and additional immunostaining was performed, which revealed high-grade adenocarcinoma with tumor cells positive for PAX8 (Figure 1B), p53, and WT1 and negative for GATA3.

answer: High-grade serous carcinoma of gynecological origin
distractors: High-grade carcinoma of the breast with occult primary
High-grade papillary carcinoma of unknown primary
explanation: B. High-grade serous carcinoma of gynecological origin This patient underwent left axillary excisional lymph node biopsy, peritoneal washings, laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omental biopsy, and bilateral ureterolysis. Laparoscopy revealed that both ovaries were affixed to the pelvic peritoneum with adhesions, requiring bilateral ureterolysis. The uterus, cervix, and proximal fallopian tubes were surgically absent. On gross examination the distal fallopian tubes appeared unremarkable, and the left ovary appeared nodular. Given the clinical scenario, the fimbrial ends of the fallopian tubes were entirely excised and submitted for microscopic examination along with both ovaries. Microscopic examination revealed a residual 2.1-mm focus of high-grade serous carcinoma (Figure 2) involving the fimbrial end of the left fallopian tube. No omental involvement was seen. The immunostaining pattern was similar to that seen in the axillary metastasis prior to therapy. No residual carcinoma was identified in the left axillary lymph node. The patient’s cancer antigen 125 level was 13 U/mL before the surgery. Disease was staged as FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) stage IVB, and the patient received additional platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy. Test results were negative for germline pathogenic sequence variants, includingBRCA1andBRCA2. Although metastatic ovarian or tubal serous carcinoma typically first spreads locally within the abdomen or peritoneum, distal extra-abdominal involvement is well established.1An isolated axillary mass rarely presents as the initial sign of ovarian or tubal serous carcinoma, and there are few cases reported.2-4Unlike other patients, this patient was initially treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy with a presumptive diagnosis of an occult breast cancer with axillary metastasis. After histopathologic reassessment and additional immunostaining at our institution, the treatment plan was adjusted accordingly. Her initial diagnostic evaluation included clinical history, radiography, and pathologic examination. Given the pathologic findings, location of the malignant neoplasm, and positive hormone receptor expression, this case was misdiagnosed as breast cancer at the outside institution. Immunohistochemical staining was key to reaching the correct diagnosis. Clinical management of axillary nodal metastases of carcinoma of unknown primary (CUPAx) is challenging. A systematic review reported that 72% of the patients with CUPAx treated with prophylactic mastectomy had an occult primary cancer of the breast,5which implied that a thorough investigation of breast origin might be appropriate and could avoid unnecessary surgeries. In these situations, immunostaining can offer more insight but only to a limited extent. Greco et al6evaluated diagnoses based on molecular profile, immunostaining (median of 6 stains), and clinical findings, and reported that diagnoses among all 3 modalities were consistent for only 34% of the patients. Some markers may provide evidence implying the primary site; for example, TTF-1 and thyroglobulin are relatively specific for thyroid cancer, CK7 and GATA3 are highly suggestive of breast cancer, and CK7, WT1, and PAX8 are indicative of gynecological adenocarcinoma.7,8While estrogen and progesterone receptors are frequently evaluated in breast cancers, they can also be expressed in ovarian cancer, and some evidence supports their prognostic value.9,10Thus, infradiaphragmatic primary malignant neoplasm should not be completely excluded when positive hormone profiles are present. Ovarian serous papillary adenocarcinoma initially presenting as axillary lymph node metastasis is rare. When managing CUPAx, primary sites other than the breast should be explored. Thorough clinical history, physical examination, and histopathologic evaluation of the biopsy specimen in conjunction with immunostaining is invaluable in establishing a diagnosis.

scenario: A man in his early 70s with a history of permanent atrial fibrillation treated with atrioventricular junction ablation and biventricular pacemaker implantation was hospitalized with decompensated heart failure and acute kidney injury. His history was notable for nonischemic cardiomyopathy with ejection fraction of 40% and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, for which he underwent single-lung transplant 9 years prior. Following diuresis and medical optimization, repeated echocardiogram showed a newly depressed ejection fraction (30%). His electrocardiogram (ECG) was notable for alternating QRS morphologies (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) pacing vector was programmed from LV tip to right ventricular (RV) lead ring. During pacemaker threshold testing, a change in QRS morphology was observed as the output was reduced (Figure 1B). Chest radiography revealed severe right pulmonary fibrosis leading to ipsilateral mediastinal shift and pacemaker lead position unchanged from implantation.
explanation: C. Change the LV pacing configuration The diagnosis of anodal capture is strongly suggested by the sudden change in QRS configuration during the LV threshold test (Figure 1B). Further, LV pacing should produce a right bundle branch block morphology (predominantly positive QRS in V1), which is not observed and raises the possibility of anodal capture. In the above LV threshold test, the paced vector (from LV lead to RV lead) resulted in concurrent capture of both the LV and RV tissue at high output. At diminishing output, left ventricular capture was lost while RV capture (anodal capture) persisted. This RV capture QRS morphology was identical to the QRS morphology when pacing from the RV lead. This is consistent with anodal stimulation, defined as pure or predominant RV capture when LV pacing. Cardiac electrical dyssynchrony is a cause of mechanical inefficiency and worsening heart failure. Placement of RV and LV leads allows for electrical resynchronization with a biventricular pacemaker. LV leads can pace in multiple configurations to avoid phrenic nerve capture or areas of scar. One common pacing configuration is to drive electrical current from the LV lead (cathode) to the RV lead (anode). When the LV tissue is diseased and difficult to excite electrically, this pacing configuration is susceptible to RV myocardial capture without LV myocardial excitation,1,2a phenomenon originally termedanodal capture.3 Identification of anodal capture requires close examination of the surface ECG by the treating physician. A biventricular pacemaker is unable to detect this phenomenon and will give a false sense of reassurance that resynchronization is occurring. In this patient’s case, device interrogation suggested that effective biventricular pacing was occurring 98% of the time while the surface ECG demonstrated that this number was closer to 66%. Previous studies have demonstrated that unrecognized anodal capture can account for failure to respond to resynchronization therapy.4,5The preferred treatment for this problem is to adjust the pacing configuration to exclude the RV lead. Of note, while this patient had a bipolar LV lead, more modern quadripolar LV leads allow multiple LV-only pacing configurations that prevent anodal capture by obviating LV to RV pacing. Finally, anodal capture is seen almost exclusively in pacemakers as the large defibrillation coil in implantable cardioverter-defibrillator leads requires much higher current to excite the RV myocardium.6 For this patient, the LV pacing configuration was changed to a true bipolar LV configuration (LV distal to proximal electrode) and a pure LV capture morphology was observed (Figure 2). Unfortunately, the patient died of complications from recurrent diverticulitis with perforation, precluding repeated echocardiographic assessment of his cardiomyopathy following adjustment of his pacing configuration.

scenario: A patient in their 20s presented to the emergency department with presyncope, hives, and nausea after walking outside in the cold. On arrival, their pulse was 120 beats per minute; blood pressure, 85/52 mm Hg; respiratory rate, 20 breaths per minute; oxygen saturation, 100% with a nonrebreather mask; and temperature, 36.8° C. The patient was in moderate respiratory distress, and chest auscultation revealed bilateral wheezing. They were treated for presumed anaphylaxis with 0.5 mg of epinephrine intramuscularly. Immediately after the administration of epinephrine, they developed a headache, nausea, and chest pain. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) was obtained 5 minutes later (Figure 1). The patient had persistent hypotension.

options.C: Give a second dose of 0.5 mg of intramuscular epinephrine
options.D: Administer 100 to 200 µg of intravenous phenylephrine

answer: Give a second dose of 0.5 mg of intramuscular epinephrine
distractors: Administer 100 to 200 µg of intravenous phenylephrine
explanation: Kounis syndrome (acute coronary vasospasm associated with anaphylactoid response) C. Give a second dose of 0.5 mg of intramuscular epinephrine Kounis syndrome is a pathological state of acute coronary vasospasm with mast cell degranulation and interaction with other inflammatory cells secondary to allergic or hypersensitivity and anaphylactic or anaphylactoid insults.1,2The inflammatory mediators involved include histamine, arachidonic acid, neutral protease, and platelet-activating factors.1,3Coronary arteries can be the primary site during anaphylaxis and result in Kounis syndrome manifestations.1,3Kounis syndrome can be precipitated by many factors, including angioedema, urticaria, hay fever, food allergy,Hymenopterastings, latex, and drugs.1,2 Three variants of Kounis syndrome have been described. Type 1 includes patients with normal or near-normal coronary arteries without predisposing factors for coronary artery disease, in whom the acute release of inflammatory mediators induce coronary artery spasm attributable to endothelial dysfunction with or without an increase of cardiac enzymes and troponins.1Type 2 includes quiescent preexisting atheromatous disease, in whom acute release of inflammatory mediators induce coronary artery spasm with plaque erosion or rupture, manifesting as acute myocardial infarction.1,4Type 3 includes patients with coronary artery stent thrombosis.4 A high index of suspicion is of paramount importance, since the diagnosis might be easily overlooked.5In the settings of allergic reactions, the presence of a cardiac symptom profile, such as acute chest pain, chest discomfort, dyspnea, palpitations, tachycardia or bradycardia, hypotension, cold extremities, diaphoresis, or cardiac arrest, must raise the suspicion for Kounis syndrome.1 The ECG may show a variety of abnormalities, including ST-segment depression or elevation, atrial fibrillation, sinus bradycardia or tachycardia, T-wave flattening or inversion, atrioventricular block, bigeminal rhythm, ventricular ectopic beats, and ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.1Serum levels of tryptase are elevated during an episode.3However, cardiac injury biomarkers, such as cardiac enzymes and troponins, may or may not be elevated.3 The management of Kounis syndrome includes treatment of both anaphylactic shock (initially with intramuscular epinephrine) and acute coronary syndrome.4Type 1 is managed with intravenous corticosteroids, H1 and H2 antihistamines, and analgesia. Type 2 is managed as per the acute coronary event protocol, along with corticosteroids and antihistamines. Type 3 requires urgent harvest of the intrastent thrombus along with corticosteroids and antihistamines. The use of additional drugs must be done cautiously, because nitroglycerine causes hypotension, β-blockers can cause coronary artery spasm, and morphine might result in mast cell degranulation.5After the resolution of the acute event, a full cardiology workup, including 12-lead ECG, echocardiogram, and evaluation for modifiable cardiac risk factors, must be performed, along with follow-up with an allergy or immunology specialist.3 The patient’s presentation was consistent with anaphylaxis and possibly cold-induced urticaria. In the emergency department, they were treated with intramuscular epinephrine, methylprednisolone, ondansetron, diphenhydramine, and famotidine, with improvement. After the resolution of symptoms, a repeated ECG showed resolution of a multilead ST-segment depression (Figure 2). The patient had normal biochemistry test results, except for an elevated high-sensitivity troponin I level of 486.0 ng/L (normal range, ≤26 ng/L; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1.0), which normalized within 16 hours during admission. The presentation was consistent with Kounis syndrome or anaphylactic coronary artery vasospasm, given the presence of anaphylaxis and ECG changes. They had an uncomplicated short admission to the internal medicine service. After consultation with the cardiology service, it was decided not to pursue coronary angiography, since symptoms had resolved and ECG and troponin results had normalized. On discharge, they were referred to an allergist and a medical genetics consultant, with instructions to carry an EpiPen always.

scenario: A 41-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1clevel of 16.8% (reference, 4.0%-5.6%) 1 month prior to admission presented to the emergency department with 1 week of generalized weakness. His temperature was 38.5 °C (101.3 °F); blood pressure, 125/75 mm Hg; heart rate, 95/min; respiratory rate, 24/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. His voice was muffled and his speech was dysarthric. He appeared lethargic but had no focal neurologic deficits. Physical examination findings were normal except for tonsillar edema. White blood cell count was 13.4 ×103/μL (reference, 4-11 ×103/μL); blood glucose level, 274 mg/dL (15.21 mmol/L) (reference, 70-100 mg/dL [3.89-5.55 mmol/L]); serum creatinine level, 0.9 mg/dL (79.56 μmol/L) (reference, 0.4-1.3 mg/dL [35.36-114.92 μmol/L]); bicarbonate level, 9 mmol/L (reference, 20-30 mmol/L); arterial pH, 7.21 (reference, 7.35-7.45); β-hydroxybutyric acid level, 58.2 mg/dL (5590 μmol/L) (reference, <2.81 mg/dL [269.9 μmol/L]); and serum anion gap, 21 (reference, 7-17). Findings on a chest radiograph were normal. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck with intravenous contrast showed mucosal thickening of the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and prominence of the adenoids and palatine tonsils. Flexible laryngoscopy showed patent nasal sinuses and mucosal edema without abscess or necrosis. He was treated with intravenous fluids and with insulin, vancomycin (1 g intravenously every 12 hours), and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g intravenously every 6 hours). On hospital day 2, his temperature was 38.9 °C (102 °F). A repeat computed tomography scan of the neck demonstrated soft-tissue gas in the nasopharynx and prevertebral fascia (Figure, left panel). Flexible laryngoscopy revealed necrotic tissue throughout the nasopharynx. Emergent transnasal endoscopic debridement of the maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoid sinuses was performed. Sinus mucosal samples grewCandida albicansin fungal cultures, and histopathology identified numerous broad, nonseptate right-angled hyphae and fruiting bodies (Figure, right panel).

options.C: Order fluconazole (200 mg orally daily for 14 days)
options.D: Prescribe prednisone (40 mg orally daily for 5 days)

answer: Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily)
distractors: Order fluconazole (200 mg orally daily for 14 days)
Prescribe prednisone (40 mg orally daily for 5 days)
explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

scenario: A 70-year-old woman with an ocular history of primary open-angle glaucoma on latanoprost, bilateral trabeculectomies, and argon laser trabeculoplasties presented with several months of worsening vision in the left eye. On examination, her best-corrected distance visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/60 OS (baseline 20/40 OU). Pupils were equally round and reactive, without afferent pupillary defect. Findings of Amsler grid testing were notable for a small area of distortion inferiorly in the left eye. Intraocular pressures (IOPs) were 13 mm Hg in both eyes. Findings of anterior segment examination were unremarkable. Findings of dilated fundus examination were notable for cup-disc ratio of 0.9 in the right eye and 0.85 in the left eye with temporal thinning, stable from prior, and new intraretinal thickening in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging of the left eye revealed schiticlike separation of the outer plexiform and outer nuclear layers extending from the temporal edge of the optic nerve head to the fovea (Figure 1A), continuous with the peripapillary nerve sheath.

options.D: Genetic testing for the RS1 gene

distractors: Genetic testing for the RS1 gene
explanation: Macular retinoschisis in the setting of glaucomatous optic atrophy The patient’s decreased vision was due to macular retinoschisis, an abnormal splitting of the neuroretina associated with glaucomatous optic atrophy. Observation (choice C) is correct because the patient noted only mild distortion, and retinoschisis can remain stable1or resolve spontaneously2,3in up to 40% of cases.3Schisis can resolve after vitrectomy,1so surgery (choice A) could be pursued if symptoms worsened. Barrier laser (choice B), as described by Prinzi et al,4has been used to treat retinoschisis in glaucoma; however, peripapillary laser photocoagulation carries risk of vision loss and the patient had only a 2-line decrease in vision. Testing for theRS1gene (choice D) would be indicated if X-linked retinoschisis was suspected; however, this disease appears almost exclusively in boys. Retinoschisis is rare in patients with glaucoma, with a reported rate of 5.9%3in 1 study. In this study, retinoschisis in glaucoma originated from the optic disc and overlapped with retinal nerve fiber layer defects, suggesting that schisis correlates with glaucomatous damage to the optic nerve head. Similarly, patients with schisis had worse visual field mean deviations compared with patients without.3Approximately one-third of eyes with schisis also had an acquired optic disc pit (aODP).3The relationship between glaucoma, aODPs, and retinoschisis is unclear. aODPs may represent areas of increased susceptibility owing to damage from glaucoma5and could be an entry point for liquified vitreous to enter the retina, initiating retinoschisis.6Therefore, the presence of an aODP in a patient with glaucoma could increase the likelihood of retinoschisis development. The patient had an optic disc pit that was visible on OCT imaging at the time of schisis onset (Figure 1B). The contribution of IOP to retinoschisis in glaucoma is not well understood. In 1 study, patients with glaucoma with retinoschisis at the initiation of the study had higher IOPs than patients without retinoschisis.3However, retinoschisis has also been reported in normal tension glaucoma,7suggesting high IOP is not a requisite for retinoschisis development. Patients who developed retinoschisis over time did not have changes in IOP before and after retinoschisis development, suggesting IOP fluctuations are not causative.3Interestingly, resolution of retinoschisis was associated with either trabeculectomy or the initiation of IOP-lowering medications. Similarly, there are case reports of retinoschisis resolving after glaucoma surgery.1,8In this patient, IOP had been well controlled prior to schisis development and no trigger could be identified, suggesting that it was the result of chronic glaucomatous damage rather than an acute process. In conclusion, the development of macular retinoschisis is associated with glaucoma and can cause decreased visual acuity in a patient with glaucoma, even with well-controlled IOP. Mild vision loss can be managed conservatively with observation. The patient was monitored with serial OCT imaging, which showed gradual improvement of the schisis over an 18-month period (Figure 2), with residual persistence along the nasal edge of the macula and return of visual acuity to baseline of 20/40 OU. The patient’s glaucoma continued to be successfully managed medically.

scenario: A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive skin discoloration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

scenario: A 5-month-old boy presented to the emergency department with acute oropharyngeal bleeding that self-resolved. Prior to presentation, he had a several-month history of slow feeding and intermittent noisy breathing. Physical examination revealed inspiratory stridor that was worse when supine. Bedside flexible endoscopy findings revealed a fleshy supraglottic mass obscuring a view of the glottis. The patient’s airway was secured in the operating room with an endotracheal tube over a 0° Hopkins rod. The mass was pedunculated on the lingual surface of the epiglottis and had areas of high vascularity and other areas of thrombosis (Figure, A). The vallecula, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, glottis, and subglottis were otherwise uninvolved. A biopsy was obtained, and pathology results revealed relatively high proliferation of small, irregular vessels with plump endothelial cells staining positive for glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) (Figure, B and C).
explanation: Infantile hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that affect up to 5% of children.1Studies report a higher incidence in White, female, and low-birth-weight infants. They are not present at birth but typically present by 1 month of age and rapidly proliferate in the first few months of life. This is then followed by slow involution over the course of years. Histologically, they are characterized by proliferation of endothelial cells that are GLUT1 positive. Early samples may appear somewhat solid. Perineurial invasion is relatively common and should not be regarded as evidence of malignant neoplasm. Mast cells may be numerous. Infantile hemangiomas should be differentiated from congenital hemangiomas, which are present at birth, do not proliferate, and do not express GLUT1.1 Treatment of infantile hemangioma is recommended if it causes pain, bleeding, disfigurement, or functional impairment. Propranolol is often the first-line medical therapy, followed by corticosteroids. Intralesional steroid injection, topical timolol, and laser therapy may also be considered. Early surgical treatment is usually used if pharmacotherapy has failed or if the lesion is focal and favorable for resection.2 Airway hemangiomas require prompt treatment because of the risk of airway obstruction. They are most often located in the subglottis, and infants usually present with stridor.3There should be a high index of suspicion for airway hemangioma in a patient with airway symptoms and segmental hemangioma in a beard distribution4or PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa malformations, hemangioma, arterial anomalies, coarctation of the aorta/cardiac defects, and eye abnormalities).5A case of bleeding as the presenting symptom of epiglottic hemangioma was previously reported 30 years ago.6Systemic propranolol is an effective treatment of most airway hemangiomas and is recommended as the first-line treatment.7-9However, multimodality therapy may be necessary in cases refractory to propranolol. In this case, the patient was kept intubated, and attempts were made to initiate systemic propranolol therapy. However, the patient was unable to tolerate it owing to hypotension and bradycardia. As such, the patient returned to the operating room for excision of the mass, which was achieved under suspension microlaryngoscopy. The patient was reexamined under anesthesia 8 weeks later with no recurrence of the lesion and slight scarring of the aryepiglottic folds.

scenario: A 56-year-old woman presented at the clinic for follow-up of metastatic hormone receptor–positive,ERBB2-negative breast cancer. She had locally advanced disease that was invading the skin overlying her right breast and metastatic disease to the thoracic and lumbar spine, liver, and mediastinal, axillary, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Her disease had progressed after receiving first-line therapy with palbociclib and anastrozole. Subsequent treatments with fulvestrant and paclitaxel were also followed by progressive disease. She received treatment with capecitabine; after 6 weeks of treatment, she developed some redness on her hands and feet that resolved on its own. She then presented to the clinic with pruritic, erythematous, scaly macules and papules on her forearms, faces, chest, and upper back (Figure). The rash had been present for 3 weeks and had recently worsened. Her palms and soles were spared. The rash did not respond to treatment with topical clindamycin, oral solumedrol, or doxycycline. distractors: Cutaneous deposits of metastatic breast cancer
explanation: B. Inflammation of actinic keratoses Capecitabine is an orally bioavailable prodrug of fluorouracil that was initially approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for treating breast and colorectal cancer and has since gained additional indications for various solid tumor cancers. After metabolism to active fluorouracil in the target tissue, the drug exhibits a cytotoxic effect through incorporation within the DNA, which is followed by strand breaks, inhibition of RNA synthesis, and inhibition of thymidylate synthase.1,2There are several cutaneous adverse effects associated with capecitabine, such as palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, vitiligo, pruritus, dermatitis, alopecia, onycholysis, and the inflammation of preexisting actinic keratoses (AKs). Actinic keratoses result from atypical proliferation of keratinocytes, with the potential for malignant transformation. They occur predominantly on chronic sun-exposed skin areas, such as the balding scalp, face, and dorsal forearms and hands, and are the most common premalignant skin condition in elderly individuals.2Many treatments exist for AKs, of which one of the most used and successful is topical fluorouracil.3 Shortly after US Food and Drug Administration approval, cases describing inflammation of AKs in patients undergoing treatment with capecitabine were published.2-6In 2020, a systemic review described the available evidence for the use of capecitabine for preventing and treating AKs, as well as its use for chemoprevention of cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas in solid organ transplant recipients.7The review comprised 8 case reports of AK inflammation, with the onset of dermatologic changes ranging from 4 days to 6 weeks after receiving treatment with capecitabine. After initial inflammation of the AK lesions, the typical course includes gradual healing and disappearance during the coming days to weeks. In described cases, some patients were prescribed topical corticosteroids for symptomatic relief, but its use was not universal. Antoniolli and colleagues8published a similar literature review and described a tendency for older studies to have included discontinuation of the drug, with a trend toward a treat through approach more recently. In all cases that reported outcomes, there was a partial or complete resolution of the inflammation of the AKs. Thus, this effect should potentially be considered therapeutic, and treatment with capecitabine should not necessarily be discontinued. The underlying mechanism for the inflammation of AKs with capecitabine is similar to the direct cytotoxic effect seen in any cancer treated with fluorouracil. The interference of DNA and RNA synthesis via inhibition of thymidylate synthase that causes double-stranded DNA breaks is key to its cytotoxic mechanism of action.1,9When administered systemically, capecitabine exhibits preferential accumulation in areas of active cell proliferation.8This is associated with amplified responses in the skin and the resultant inflammation of AKs, while sparing normal skin. A pathologically distinct yet phenotypically similar phenomenon has been described in radiation recall dermatitis. It is defined as the recalling of an effect that is similar to an acute radiation reaction in an area of previous irradiation.10Capecitabine has been a medication recently implicated in this phenomenon.10The underlying pathophysiology is poorly understood, but it is theorized that upregulation of thymidine phosphorylase plays a role in the neoangiogenesis and preferential accumulation of capecitabine in previously irradiated tissue. The current patient was prescribed triamcinolone, 0.1%, cream for symptomatic relief. She did not experience further episodes of inflammation with subsequent treatment cycles of capecitabine, and the skin lesions eventually resolved.

B, Sagittal cut of neck CT scan showing 2-cm radiodense osseous foreign body in the upper cervical esophagus at C6 level (arrowhead). C, Coronal cut of CT scan showing gas in the thyroid gland (arrowheads).
scenario: A healthy patient in their teens presented to the emergency department with high-grade fever (38.7 °C), neck pain, and a foreign body sensation in the throat after eating chicken 3 days prior. Laboratory investigations demonstrated an elevated leukocyte count (22 500/µL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Lateral soft tissue radiography showed a radio-opaque foreign body at the level of C6. Computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed a 2-cm radio-opaque osseous foreign body at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle with signs of esophageal perforation, including air leak tracking toward the left lobe of the thyroid gland (Figure, A and B). The patient was brought to the operating room, and the esophageal foreign body was successfully removed. Postoperatively, the patient continued to become febrile despite intravenous antibiotic therapy. A repeated CT scan of the neck and chest was done (Figure, C).
explanation: This case is a great example of the clinical implications of cervical anatomy. The fascial layers of the neck are complex and can be divided into the superficial and deep layers. The deep cervical fascia can be further classified into the superficial (investing), middle, and deep layers. The middle layer is subdivided into the muscular and visceral layers, with the latter surrounding the anterior viscera of the neck, including the thyroid gland, trachea, and esophagus.1Given that both the esophagus and thyroid gland are enveloped in the visceral portion of the middle layer of the deep cervical fascia, one can anticipate how an esophageal perforation can result in air infiltrating the thyroid parenchyma. The resulting inflammation then leads to the clinical picture of emphysematous thyroiditis (ET).1,2 Signs and symptoms of ET that have been described in the literature include severe neck pain, dysphagia, dysphonia, and stridor.1Additionally, patients may have a toxic appearance and exhibit signs of tachycardia, high-grade fever, and rigors.2,3Physical examination may reveal neck swelling and cellulitis.2,3Crepitus may not be appreciated due to the deep location of the thyroid gland within the fascial layers of the neck.3 Imaging studies of the neck showing gas in the thyroid region are pathognomonic for acute ET.2Laboratory test results may show a significantly elevated white blood cell count along with other inflammatory markers.3In addition, results of thyroid function tests and thyroid antibody testing may be initially normal; however, the patient reported by Gigot et al3developed hypothyroidism 4 months later. This may be explained by the pyogenic destruction of thyroid tissue.3On the other hand, the current patient exhibited laboratory results indicating hyperthyroidism; however, the patient did not experience any signs or symptoms of hyperthyroidism. The most common cause among cases reviewed in the literature was infection withClostridium perfringens.3In addition, multinodular goiter was found in 4 of the 6 patients reported by Gigot et al,3which places these patients at higher risk of developing an anaerobic infection due to the increased incidence of areas with anoxic thyroid tissue. Penetrating injury to the neck was another cause that led to ET reported in the literature, although the injury was not associated with injury to the esophagus or trachea.2 Treatment of ET is aimed at treating the cause and may be either medical or surgical.2,3The majority of patients (5 out of 6) who were reviewed by Gigot et al3underwent incision and drainage, and 4 also received antibiotics. One patient received medical therapy to treat ET and needed large doses of intramuscular penicillin.3Meanwhile, the patient reported by Karadağ et al,2who developed ET after a penetrating neck trauma, was treated conservatively without any surgical intervention and made an unremarkable recovery after close follow-up. The current patient remained afebrile after the fourth postoperative day and made an unremarkable recovery for the remainder of the hospital stay. Esophageal perforation showed evidence of closure on postoperative day 9. The patient was therefore deemed fit for discharge and was sent home and prescribed oral amoxicillin-clavulanate treatment for 7 days. A follow-up appointment with otolaryngology 3 weeks after discharge revealed that the patient was doing well, with no evidence of dysphagia, neck pain, or fever, and had an unremarkable physical examination. Results of repeated thyroid function tests during the patient’s follow-up with endocrinology 6 weeks after discharge showed almost complete normalization.

scenario: A man in his 40s was seen in clinic for a long history of palpitations. He had a history of cardiac arrest after receiving adenosine for sustained supraventricular tachycardia and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. The patient was also noted to have episodes of atrial flutter. Transthoracic echocardiogram displayed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 63% and mild aortic and mitral regurgitation. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging in sinus rhythm showed mild left ventricle thickening (up to 14 mm) and was otherwise normal. The patient was hospitalized for initiation of sotalol, given that he experienced frequent episodes of atrial arrhythmia.Figure 1A shows sinus rhythm prior to sotalol initiation.Figure 1B shows telemetry during administration of sotalol.
explanation: Latent accessory pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) B. Electrophysiology study and catheter ablation Prior to sotalol loading, the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) (Figure1A) showed sinus rhythm at 57 beats per minute with a normal axis and QT interval. There were no Q waves in the lateral leads. There were inferolateral precordial T-wave abnormalities. With sotalol loading, the telemetry strip (Figure1B) revealed widening of the QRS complex. The differential diagnosis included (1) rate-related aberrancy, (2) idioventricular rhythm, (3) phase 4 aberrancy, and (4) preexcitation from an atrioventricular pathway. Phase 3 or 4 aberrancy was unlikely because the sinus rate had not changed significantly. An idioventricular rhythm resulting in this finding would have to be perfectly isorhythmic to maintain constant PR intervals. The short, fixed PR interval with wide QRS complex makes ventricular preexcitation from an atrioventricular pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) the most likely diagnosis.1Electrophysiology study and catheter ablation provide high likelihood of cure. Amiodarone is not indicated in a young patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome; ST segment changes are due to altered ventricular repolarization owing to preexcitation rather than ischemia. Exercise treadmill testing is not useful with lack of ischemia or exposure to medications with use dependence (class I). The ECG initially did not show clear ventricular preexcitation. An accessory pathway that is not capable of antegrade conduction will not be apparent on an ECG in sinus rhythm; this is termedconcealed preexcitation.2However, with sotalol loading, anterograde conduction with delta waves develops in this patient without a change in heart rate. Absent delta waves in the presence of an accessory pathway capable of anterograde conduction has been termedlatent preexcitation.3The proposed mechanism for this phenomenon is due to relative conduction times from the sinus node through the atrioventricular node vs across the atrium and the accessory pathway. Conditions that may cause latent preexcitation include left-lateral pathways, delay in intra-atrial conduction time, or increased left-atrial size. Some evidence exists that this phenomenon may occur when autonomic influences on the pathway and on atrioventricular nodal conduction are opposite.4Additionally, concealed retrograde conduction into the accessory pathway during sinus rhythm could prevent preexcitation and eliminate delta waves. Sotalol has been studied for treatment of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia  in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome but has not been reported to reveal a latent accessory pathway. Sotalol causes an increase in the retrograde effective refractory period of accessory pathways, whereas changes in the anterograde refractory periods were more variable.5,6It is unlikely that sotalol improved conduction in the accessory pathway. Instead, sotalol slows atrioventricular nodal conduction and may prevent concealed retrograde conduction into the pathway in a manner analogous to transseptal concealed conduction for perpetuation of bundle-branch block. Repeated 12-lead ECG confirmed manifest preexcitation (short PR intervals and delta waves,Figure 2). Negative delta waves in leads II, III, and aVF and QRS transition between V1and V2argues for a posteroseptal pathway.7The patient then developed a narrow-complex short RP tachycardia showing negative P waves in the inferior leads consistent with a posterior accessory pathway-mediated orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia. The tachycardia was terminated with the Valsalva maneuver. After providing consent, the patient underwent successful catheter ablation of the posteroseptal pathway and cavotricuspid isthmus (for typical right-atrial flutter). The successful ablation site was the anterior floor of the coronary sinus body, about 1 to 2 cm from the coronary sinus ostium. Sotalol treatment was discontinued, and the patient was discharged with metoprolol and lisinopril therapy.

scenario: A 75-year-old man presented with several weeks of intermittent headache that had progressed to severe, persistent headache with right eye pain. He had hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation. He denied tobacco, alcohol, or drug use. A neurological examination was notable for disorientation to the month, deficits in short-term memory, and an upward drift of the left arm. Cranial nerve, sensory, coordination, and deep tendon reflex examinations were normal. He walked with a slightly wide but steady gait. His serum red and white blood cell counts, coagulation profile, and electrolyte levels were within normal limits. Blood cultures had negative results. A 24-hour electroencephalogram showed right hemispheric slowing and multiple right centroparietal seizures of 1 minute each, without noticeable clinical correlates. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain was remarkable for a large T2-hyperintense lesion in the right temporoparietal region, with an increased diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) signal (low apparent diffusion coefficient), a low signal on susceptibility-weighted imaging, increased T1 signal intensity in and around the lesion, and a contrast-enhancing rim with leptomeningeal enhancement (Figure 1). A smaller satellite lesion with a similar MRI profile was noted inferiorly in the right anterior temporal lobe. A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis did not show any metastatic disease. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profile showed a normal red blood cell count and protein and glucose levels and a mildly elevated white blood cell count of 11 cells/μL (to convert to cells × 109/L, multiply by 0.001). The fluid was absent oligoclonal bands and had negative bacterial and fungal culture results, a meningitis-encephalitis polymerase chain reaction panel, and a paraneoplastic panel. Cytology and flow cytometry had negative results. The patient then underwent surgical biopsy of the temporoparietal lesion.
explanation: C. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy–related inflammation The differential diagnosis of rim-enhancing lesions with increased DWI signal and low apparent diffusion coefficient in the central nervous system chiefly consists of neoplastic (primary and metastatic), infectious (bacterial and fungal abscesses), inflammatory or autoimmune (multiple sclerosis and granulomatous disease), and vascular (subacute infarction and resolving hemorrhage) causes.1,2In this case, no primary cancer was identified on a computed tomography panscan, and results of CSF studies were largely negative; thus, neoplastic and infectious causes were less likely. This patient had clinical and imaging features more consistent with cerebral amyloid angiopathy–related inflammation (CAA-ri). The key to definitive diagnosis was lesion biopsy, which showed gliotic brain tissue with blood and mixed inflammatory infiltrates (neutrophils, lymphocytes, and foamy macrophages) (Figure 2). Granulation tissue with prominent vasculature was present; however, no active disruption or fibrinoid necrosis was identified within the vessel walls. The astrocytes were reactive but evenly spaced. No mitotic figures were seen. An infectious disease workup had negative results (including gram, Gomori methenamine–silver, and acid-fast stains). Notably, pink amorphous material was identified within the vessel walls and stained positive for β amyloid (Figure 2). These findings are consistent with CAA-ri.3 Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) most commonly presents with lobar hemorrhage, reflecting the underlying distribution of vascular amyloid deposits.4However, CAA-ri represents a distinct subtype of CAA in which amyloid deposition is associated with a cellular inflammatory response.5Diagnosis of CAA-ri is challenging, yet critical, given its therapeutic potential; CAA-ri is clinically characterized by subacute headache, cognitive decline, and seizures.6A brain MRI typically shows evidence of hemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging sequences and perilesional patchy or confluent white matter hyperintensities (representing vasogenic edema) on T2 sequences.7Leptomeningeal enhancement may be seen in up to 70% of patients with CAA-ri.8Analysis of CSF is often nonrevealing but may show a mild pleocytosis and/or elevated protein levels. Diagnostic criteria for CAA-ri were set forth by Chung and colleagues3with 5 supporting items: (1) age of 40 years or more; (2) presence of either headache, decreased consciousness, behavioral change, focal neurological signs, or seizures, none of which are attributable to hemorrhage; (3) an MRI with white matter lesions; (4) presence of cerebral macrobleeds, cerebral microbleeds, or cortical superficial siderosis; and (5) absence of neoplastic, infectious, or other causative mechanisms. The criteria were recently validated and showed a sensitivity and specificity of 82% and 97%, respectively, for the probable diagnosis of CAA-ri.7 There is no cure for CAA, but early recognition of CAA-ri is critical, given its treatable nature with prolonged immunosuppression.5The initial therapy choice is often corticosteroids; steroid-sparing agents have been used successfully for longer-term treatment.3,9Up to 75% will improve with treatment, but roughly half of these patients will eventually relapse.3,9 This case highlights that a combination of clinical, diagnostic, and imaging features can be used to suspect the diagnosis of CAA-ri. Currently, pathology is needed for a definitive diagnosis, and following negative infectious and neoplastic workup results, a biopsy should be strongly considered. Future research may clarify if advanced imaging, such as amyloid positron emission tomography, may be useful in diagnosing CAA-ri.10Prompt treatment with immunosuppressive therapy is essential to give the patient the best chance for clinical improvement. In this case, the patient was initially treated with high-dose corticosteroids followed by a steroid taper. His cognition and headaches dramatically improved. Unfortunately, the patient presented again 3 weeks after discharge with worsening cognition and seizures and did not survive his second hospitalization.

caption: Clinical images of keratotic papules diffusely distributed on an extremity, original (A) and magnified (B).
scenario: A woman in her 50s presented with a 3-month history of rapidly spreading intensively pruritic papules on her extremities. The lesions consisted of scattered, erythematous, annular papules measuring up to 5 mm wide (Figure 1). Further examination revealed a few asymptomatic brown flat papules scattered on her face; the palms, soles, and oral mucosa were not involved. The patient had no remarkable medical or family history and was not concurrently being treated with any medications. She had been previously diagnosed with eczema and treated with topical steroid ointments and oral compound glycyrrhizin tablets, which had no obvious effect. Laboratory investigations, including routine blood, liver and kidney function, antistreptolysin O, C-reactive protein, antinuclear antibody, and rheumatoid factor tests, disclosed no abnormal findings. A biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathologic examination.
explanation: C. Eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis (EPPP) The skin biopsy specimen from an annular lesion revealed mild hyperkeratosis accompanied by parakeratosis, atrophy of the epidermis, well-developed cornoid lamellae with a decreased granular layer, individual cell dyskeratosis, and vacuolar degeneration of the basal cell layer (Figure 2A). There was a slight infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and eosinophils in the upper dermis (Figure 2B). A diagnosis of EPPP was established. Six months after the patient’s first visit, the papules began to subside spontaneously without any medication, leaving sporadic brown annular keratotic lesions. Eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis is a rare variant of porokeratosis, presenting with acute exacerbation of annular papules surrounded by a distinctive hyperkeratotic ridgelike border accompanied by severe pruritus; it has also been called eruptive disseminated porokeratosis (EDP).1-3Shoimer and colleagues categorized EDP into 4 subtypes: paraneoplastic, immunosuppressed, inflammatory, and other type.1In the present case, the asymptomatic brown papules on the patient’s face were consistent with disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis; however, the lesions distributed over the non−sun-exposed flexor surfaces of the extremities differed from this condition. According to Shoimer and colleagues’ proposed classification, the lesions on the extremities should be considered to be an EDP of the inflammatory subtype. Histologically, the presence of a cornoid lamella and a dermal inflammatory infiltrate are the most frequent findings.2Approximately 25% to 50% of patients with EPPP show additional eosinophilic infiltration in the vicinity of blood vessels in the upper dermis.3 Differential diagnoses of EPPP include annular lichen planus (ALP), perforating granuloma annulare (PGA), and atypical pityriasis rosea (APR). A rare clinical variant of lichen planus, ALP presents with a slightly raised annular edge and central clearing.4The annular edge is typically purple to white and the central portion is hyperpigmented or skin colored.4Individual lesions range in size from 0.5 to 2.5 cm.4Generalized eruptions of ALP are rarely described.4Few patients have pruritus.4Sites of involvement include the axilla, penis, extremities, groin, and other areas.4Histologically, ALP is associated with hyperkeratosis without parakeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, and a bandlike lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction, whereas EPPP is associated with cornoid lamella with a decreased granular layer.5 Another differential diagnosis is PGA, which may present as an umbilicated papule with a central crust or hyperkeratotic core on the extremities or trunk with lesions that become pustular or ulcerate; it is a condition more commonly reported in children.6Eruptions are usually asymptomatic, although pruritus and pain have been reported.7Histologically, PGA is characterized by mucinous collagen degeneration surrounded by palisading granulomas with transepithelial elimination of altered collagen.6 In diagnosing EPPP, it is also important to exclude APR, which commonly presents as papular, vesicular, and purpuric lesions.8Most of the lesions follow a course similar to the classic form of pityriasis rosea.9A herald patch is an important marker, which is seen in most of the atypical cases, and atypia is rare in herald patches.8The involvement of the face, scalp, hands, and feet is unusual, and pityriasis rosea of the fingers, scalp, eyelids, and penis is exceptional.9Itching may be severe, with pain and burning sensation in some cases.9Histopathologic examination reveals focal parakeratosis in the epidermis, spongiosis, extravasation of red blood cells, and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.8 There is no standard treatment for EPPP. Topical corticosteroids and antihistamines are the most frequently used treatment, but response is often poor.2Topical fluorouracil, etretinate, assisted freezing, and laser therapy have been used, but their effectiveness is unsatisfactory.2A topical vitamin D3analogue, maxacalcitol, may be effective against pruritic papules.3 Because EPPP may be associated with various neoplasms (31% of cases) and viral infections (2% of cases), screening for malignant neoplasms is recommended. For 75% of EPPP cases, resolution is spontaneous after 6 months2; therefore, screening for tumors is important, if clinically indicated.2

scenario: A 50-year-old man was referred for ophthalmoplegia that developed immediately after an 8.5-hour robotic cystectomy for small cell cancer of the bladder. After recovering from anesthesia in the postanesthesia care unit, he experienced headache, facial numbness, inability to open both his eyes, and inability to move both eyes in any direction. He had a known enhancing central skull base lesion in sella turcica with compression of the optic chiasm and mild mass effect on the pons that was felt to be a pituitary macroadenoma (Figure). His baseline examination before the cystectomy showed visual acuity of 20/20 OU with intact extraocular movements and unremarkable confrontational fields, although a mild bitemporal hemianopia was seen on automated visual fields. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation. No exophthalmos was noted. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained 12 hours after symptom onset redemonstrating the large sellar mass, which no longer had central enhancement (Figure).
explanation: Based on the acute presentation of symptoms and signs starting immediately after surgery and change in the appearance of tumor on MRI (loss of central enhancement), a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy was made. The ophthalmoplegia in ocular motor apraxia can be overcome with vestibular ocular reflex, which was not the case here. The absence of exophthalmos and normal intraocular pressure argue against the diagnosis of orbital compartment syndrome. Imaging does not support the diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Pituitary apoplexy is an acute-onset syndrome due to hemorrhaging and/or infarction of the pituitary gland. Postoperative pituitary apoplexy has been reported after cardiac surgery, abdominal surgery, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic lumbar spinal fusion, and knee arthroplasty.1Risk factors proposed during surgery that could lead to pituitary apoplexy include prolonged mechanical ventilation, embolization, unstable blood pressure, anticoagulation, crystalloid hemodilution, previous treatment with dopamine agonists, and radiotherapy.2 Patients with pituitary apoplexy typically present with headaches. Cranial nerve palsies leading to ophthalmoplegia have been reported in about 50% of patients during pituitary apoplexy.1Sixty-four percent of patients can have vision loss from worsening chiasmal compression, which fortunately this patient did not have.3Early neuroimaging study is important to confirm the suspicion of pituitary apoplexy, along with urgent pituitary function tests. Computed tomography scan is often the first study performed in an acute setting and may demonstrate a variably hyperdense mass of the sella and suprasellar region in the presence of hemorrhage. MRI is the preferred study of choice with sensitivity of about 90%.4Appearance of hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy on MRI depends on the sequence and stage of hemorrhage. In the acute phase, hemorrhage is usually hypotense on T2-weighted imaging because of the presence of deoxyhemoglobin, which was not present in the present patient. Infarctive pituitary apoplexy alone, which is a rarer presentation of pituitary apoplexy, has low signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted sequences and no contrast enhancement of the tumor as seen in this patient. It may have associated rim enhancement.5 Pituitary apoplexy is a vision- and life-threatening neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Before the use of corticosteroids, mortality rates were reported to be as high as 50% because of acute adrenal insufficiency that many of these patients develop. Treatment involves urgent administration of steroids, endocrine evaluation, and urgent surgical intervention for prompt decompression based on severity of presentation. Visual recovery, with or without sequelae, is variable depending on the severity and duration of compression of the optic nerve apparatus. Ophthalmoplegia resolves in the majority of patients, but some patients can have incomplete recovery.6,7 The patient immediately started receiving intravenous corticosteroids under the guidance of endocrinology and neurosurgery. He was monitored for any endocrine deficiencies while inpatient. After no improvement in extraocular movements were noted over 5 days, the patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of pituitary tumor. Pathological evaluation of the tumor confirmed a pituitary adenoma with areas of necrosis consistent with pituitary apoplexy. Postoperative MRI showed successful resection of the large pituitary macroadenoma, with decompression of the optic chiasm. There was some residual tumor in the bilateral cavernous sinuses, basisphenoid, and along the dorsum sella. One year after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Bilateral ptosis had resolved. Extraocular movements were full and the eyes were well aligned. However, the pupils remained unresponsive to light and accommodation. The mild bitemporal hemianopsia remained unchanged from baseline on automated visual fields.

scenario: A 53-year-old man received a diagnosis of stage IV melanoma with metastatic disease to the spine and brain 3 months before presentation. Four weeks following receipt of immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab, he developed acute abdominal pain in the setting of a rapidly rising lactic acid dehydrogenase levels, prompting hospital admission. Imaging results showed mild disease progression (new ascites and periportal metabolic lymph node). Splenic infarct and portal/splenic vein thrombi were identified as etiologies of his acute pain and were presumed to be secondary to hypercoagulable state of malignancy. Over the next 3 days, he had rising serum creatinine (sCr) levels (baseline, approximately 1 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4]). The initial workup included ultrasonography and urinalysis. Ultrasonography results showed abnormal intraparenchymal flow to both kidneys without evidence of kidney artery stenosis. Urine studies were consistent with prerenal etiology, while the presence of casts suggested acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxic medications (omeprazole/pantoprazole) were discontinued. The top differential diagnoses at this juncture included contrast-induced nephropathy or immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)–induced acute interstitial nephritis, and empirical high dose steroids were prescribed. Despite observation and steroid treatment, his sCr levels continued to increase over the next 5 days, peaking at 5.8 mg/dL, and the patient progressed into anuric kidney failure, requiring hemodialysis. This prompted a kidney biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Figure). One week later, he received encorafenib, aBRAFinhibitor.1Two weeks later, the patient’s kidney function began to improve, and hemodialysis was discontinued. He continued to show gradual improvement, with a return to near baseline kidney function (sCr level, 1.3 mg/dL) approximately 6 weeks after treatment initiation.

options.A: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
options.C: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis

answer: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis
distractors: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
explanation: C. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis The kidney is an uncommon site of clinically apparent melanoma metastases. While kidney micrometastases may be found in up to half of patients with a history of melanoma on postmortem evaluation, they are typically subclinical small cortical nodules.2,3The few cases of symptomatic kidney involvement from melanoma have been secondary to large cortical masses that can be visualized on imaging.4-7Thus, symptomatic kidney micrometastases and/or isolated tumor cells with intracapillary involvement are a rare phenomenon. The patient’s biopsy findings were suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) that followed metastatic melanoma cells occluding kidney capillaries and limiting blood flow to tubules. The specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed intracapillary atypical cells with enlarged nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm (Figure, A) and diffuse mild acute tubular injury with tubular dilatation and extensive isometric cytoplasmic vacuolization of tubular epithelial cells (Figure, B), which were consistent with ATN. Intracapillary atypical cells were positive for melanin-A (Figure, C), Sry-related HMg-Box gene 10, S-100, and human melanoma black–45 stains, which indicated the presence of melanoma micrometasases. These findings may account for the abnormal intraparenchymal flow that was visualized on ultrasonography, although no positron emission tomography avidity was appreciated in the kidneys. In the setting of the patient’s clinical history, the histopathologic findings were diagnostic for ATN secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis, primarily involving the glomeruli. The typical course of ATN involves a 1- to 2-week oliguric phase, followed by a 1- to 2-week nonoliguric phase and subsequent recovery of kidney function.8The patient’s prolonged nonoliguric phase, with remarkable improvement corresponding to treatment with encorafenib, may further suggest that the etiology of his kidney injury was associated with melanoma. After starting treatment with encorafenib and being discharged from the hospital, the patient showed substantial improvement in his kidney function and overall status, no longer requiring hemodialysis. Other etiologies of ATN include kidney ischemia and nephrotoxin exposures.8The patient had no risk factors for kidney ischemia and had been adequately hydrated with intravenous fluids. Although contrast can induce ATN, the peak in sCr levels typically occurs acutely after exposure (within 48-72 hours).9However, this patient was in the hospital for several weeks, with no improvement in sCr levels until after encorafenib was administered. The patient’s other nephrotoxic exposures included proton-pump inhibitors, which are associated with allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN) rather than ATN.10 While AIN secondary to ICI therapy was also in the differential, there was no patchy edema or inflammatory cell infiltrate on pathology to support this diagnosis. Although histopathologic findings may have been affected by the course of steroids, the patient’s concomitant rapidly worsening kidney function made a diagnosis of AIN unlikely. Finally, albeit the exhaustive sampling of the biopsy cores was per protocol, there was no histopathologic evidence of microthrombi or postinfectious glomerulonephritis. This case illustrates a rare finding of metastatic melanoma with glomerular involvement followed by anuric kidney failure from ATN, with substantial recovery of kidney function with encorafenib. In conclusion, kidney metastases should be considered in patients with advanced melanoma who present with kidney failure, even if there is no visible mass on imaging. Kidney biopsy and/or treatment targeted at melanoma cells may be appropriate steps in management.

scenario: A 67-year-old woman with fibromyalgia presented with sequential bilateral vision loss. Vision decreased suddenly in the right eye 3 to 4 weeks prior and in the left eye 5 days prior. She reported left-sided scalp tenderness; jaw claudication; neck, shoulder, and low back pain; and a recent 6.8-kilogram weight loss. Visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye (OD) and hand motion in the left eye (OS). She had a left relative afferent pupillary defect, moderate dry-eye syndrome, and mild cataracts. The right optic nerve had a cup-disc ratio of 0.55 with temporal pallor and mild optic disc edema, and the left nerve had a cup-disc ratio of 0.50 with mild edema without pallor. Bilateral arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy was suspected. Expedited evaluation and treatment of giant cell arteritis (GCA) was pursued. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was elevated at 61 mm/h, whereas C-reactive protein (CRP), hemoglobin, and platelet levels were normal. She was hospitalized for empirical treatment with 1 g of intravenous methylprednisolone sodium succinate daily for 5 days. Results of a left temporal artery biopsy (TAB) were negative for GCA. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed abnormal signal and contrast enhancement within the intraorbital midportion of both optic nerves (Figure 1A and B) as well as incidental parotid gland cysts bilaterally (Figure 1C). She was discharged and was taking oral prednisone anhydrous, 60 mg daily. One month later the patient had improvement in visual acuity to 20/50 OD and 20/25 OS.

options.A: Bilateral non–arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy
options.C: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder associated with Sjögren syndrome

answer: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder associated with Sjögren syndrome
distractors: Bilateral non–arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy
explanation: C. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder associated with Sjögren syndrome The initial clinical suspicion for GCA was high given the patient’s classic presentation—a woman older than 65 years with sequential bilateral vision loss accompanied by scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, weight loss, and musculoskeletal pain suggestive of polymyalgia rheumatica. Expedited evaluation and treatment are critical in suspected GCA. Initial laboratory workup should include ESR, CRP, and platelet count tests. Chan et al1found that these 3 tests have similar sensitivity (range, 65%-71%) and specificity (range, 57%-62%) for GCA. The gold standard of GCA diagnosis is TAB, but the sensitivity is only 77%.2Empirical treatment should not be delayed for TAB because the positivity rate is similar after up to 4 weeks of systemic corticosteroid therapy.3In this clinically suspicious patient with ESR elevation but normal CRP level and platelet count and negative TAB results, GCA remained a plausible diagnosis to justify continued corticosteroid therapy. Vision loss secondary to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is generally substantial and irreversible despite corticosteroid therapy,4and treatment aims to reduce visual morbidity rather than restore vision. Accordingly, this patient underwent empirical treatment with high-dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy with the intent to preserve the remaining right eye vision. This patient’s improvement in vision was unexpected and challenged the working diagnosis of GCA (choice B). The patient also lacked the chalky optic nerve edema classically seen in GCA. On the contrary, this patient appeared to have a corticosteroid-responsive optic neuritis. A differential diagnosis might include demyelinating disease (eg, multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease [MOGAD]) and inflammatory processes (eg, neurosarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome [SS]). Investigation for alternative diagnoses was pursued. The evidence of dry-eye disease on examination and incidental bilateral parotid gland cysts on neuroimaging suggested underlying SS. Of note, parotid cysts are not specific to SS and can also be seen in benign lymphoepithelial lesions (as occur in HIV infection), sarcoidosis, Warthin tumor, and obstructive sialadenitis.5Serologic test results were positive for anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, and anti–aquaporin 4 antibodies. The patient subsequently underwent cervical and thoracic spine magnetic resonance imaging, which showed contiguous signal abnormality in the spinal cord from T1 to T3 (Figure 2). Thus, the patient was diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) associated with SS (choice C). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for anti–aquaporin 4 antibody (as used in this patient) has 97% specificity for NMOSD, and serum cell-based assays have up to 99% specificity.6Bilateral non–arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (choice A) would be unlikely in this patient who lacked the disc-at-risk configuration—crowded small nerve head with small cup-disc ratio.7 Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder may occur in association with other autoimmune diseases. Co-occurrence with SS has been described, and in patients with this co-occurrence, onset of NMOSD may precede sicca symptoms.8Other autoimmune disorders associated with NMOSD include systemic lupus erythematosus, myasthenia gravis, systemic sclerosis, and sarcoidosis.8A causal association unifying comorbid autoimmune disease and NMOSD has not been established, and it is unknown if the association is better explained by genetic tendency toward autoimmunity.8In contrast, co-occurring autoimmune disease is rare with MOGAD (choice D)9; indeed, serological testing for MOGAD was negative in this case. Initial therapy for acute episodes of NMOSD is intravenous corticosteroids. Refractory episodes may be treated with plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin.8,10Long-term therapy uses immunosuppression. First-line immunosuppressive agents include azathioprine, rituximab, and mycophenolate mofetil. Second-line agents include methotrexate, mitoxantrone, and cyclophosphamide.10 The patient was treated with immunosuppressive therapy (initially methotrexate sodium and later mycophenolate mofetil) with concurrent slow taper of oral prednisone. At the 5-month follow-up, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/60 OD and 20/30 OS.
